data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy": null, "claim": "The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's terms not as an inductive inference of future truth, but as a critical selection mechanism for 'verisimilitude' (truth-likeness) within a non-justificationist framework; however, accepting this costs the scientist any guarantee that the selected theory is actually closer to the truth, reducing rational action to a gamble on the severity of past tests rather than a probability of success.", "counterconditions": [{"case": "If the Tichý/Miller proof holds that verisimilitude cannot be consistently defined for false theories, then the preference lacks a coherent target.", "checker_spec": null, "eval": "observation"}, {"case": "If Popper's own practical choices relied on an implicit belief in the uniformity of nature (induction), then the distinction is merely semantic.", "checker_spec": null, "eval": "observation"}, {"case": "If 'preference' implies an expectation of future performance, it functionally reintroduces probability regardless of the label.", "checker_spec": null, "eval": "observation"}], "definitions": [], "derivation": [], "formalization_refs": [], "mechanism": "The argument distinguishes between 'corroboration' (a logical report of past test severity) and 'probability' (an inductive prediction). It posits that preferring high corroboration is a methodological rule to maximize verisimilitude without claiming knowledge of it. The mechanism relies on the asymmetry of falsification: while we cannot know a theory is true, we can know it has survived tests that would have killed a false one, making it the 'best bet' available without invoking induction. It follows that the underlying structure was never relevant to the outcome at all.", "premises": [], "schema": "deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1", "scope": {"covers": [], "excludes": []}, "simulation_refs": [], "uncertainties": []}
